one_liner: Q16.16 fixed-point math library in C for FPU-less targets; on 8-bit AVR, add/sub beat soft-float about 2x, mul/div lose.
what_it_does: libfixmath represents numbers as fix16_t (an int32_t in Q16.16: range about -32768 to +32767.99998, step 1/65536) and provides add, sub, mul, div and mod, saturating variants (fix16_sadd/ssub/smul/sdiv), lerp, sqrt, exp, log/log2, sin/cos/tan/asin/acos/atan/atan2, and string conversion. It is a plain C function API (fix16_mul(a, b) rather than a * b); an optional C++ wrapper class Fix16 in fix16.hpp adds operator overloads. Behaviour is tuned with compile definitions (FIXMATH_NO_OVERFLOW, FIXMATH_NO_ROUNDING, FIXMATH_NO_CACHE, FIXMATH_NO_64BIT, FIXMATH_OPTIMIZE_8BIT, FIXMATH_FAST_SIN, FIXMATH_SIN_LUT).
how_it_is_fast: On a CPU without an FPU, every float operation is a software routine that unpacks exponent and mantissa, aligns, normalises and rounds; Q16.16 add and subtract are a single 32-bit integer add plus an optional sign-based overflow check. Multiplication has three implementations chosen at compile time: a 32x32-to-64-bit multiply (fastest on Cortex-M3 per the source comment), a 32-bit-only version, and an 8-bit version for AVR that does byte-by-byte 8x8-to-16 multiplies and skips zero bytes; division has a hardware-division path and a shift-and-subtract path. Transcendentals use Taylor series (exp), a bitwise square root, polynomial sine, and optional 4096-entry memo caches (32 KB for exp, 80 KB for trig) or a 102,688-entry sine lookup table.
when_to_use: 8-bit or FPU-less 32-bit microcontrollers (AVR, Cortex-M0/M0+/M3) where the hot loop is dominated by additions and subtractions of values that fit Q16.16; the project's AVR table shows fix16_add 67 versus 135 cycles for soft-float add.

Code that must not touch floating point at all, such as Linux kernel modules (fix16 sources build under __KERNEL__ since 2022) or toolchains without soft-float support, while still needing sqrt, exp, log and trig.

Bit-reproducible results across platforms: the core functions use integer operations only, so the same inputs and compile options give the same bits everywhere (keep the same option set on every target).
Small firmware that can vendor a handful of MIT-licensed .c files and turn off the caches (FIXMATH_NO_CACHE) to fit in a few KB of RAM.
when_not_to_use: Any target with a hardware FPU (Cortex-M4F/M7, x86, aarch64): fpm's docs/performance.md (Google Benchmark, i7-5820K) reports its own Q16.16 type up to an order of magnitude slower than native float for most functions (faster only for add, sub and several power and trig functions) and libfixmath (built with FIXMATH_NO_CACHE) no faster than fpm except for exp.
Multiply- or divide-heavy code on AVR: in the project's own table fix16_mul (377 cycles) is 2.7x slower and fix16_div (637 cycles) 1.4x slower than avr-gcc soft-float multiply and divide.
Values outside about +/-32768, or computations needing more than 1/65536 resolution or float-like dynamic range (products of small numbers lose precision quickly, sin/cos error is about 2.1%).
Multithreaded code or interrupt handlers calling fix16_exp, fix16_sin/cos or fix16_atan2 with the default caches on: the caches are unsynchronised global arrays (see gotchas).
RAM-tight parts with default options: the exp and trig caches take 32 KB and 80 KB of static RAM unless FIXMATH_NO_CACHE is defined (an ATmega128 has 4 KB of internal SRAM).

integration.form: static lib (CMake target libfixmath, or drop the libfixmath/*.c and .h files into the build)
integration.dependencies: none (stdint.h, stdbool.h, limits.h; libm only for the test programs)
integration.min_toolchain: C11 per CMakeLists.txt (CMAKE_C_STANDARD 11, CMake 3.13); the code itself is C99-style; GCC-specific function attributes are applied automatically when __GNUC__ is set
integration.platforms: any; FIXMATH_NO_64BIT for compilers without uint64_t, FIXMATH_OPTIMIZE_8BIT for AVR-class 8-bit multipliers, FIXMATH_NO_HARD_DIVISION for cores without a divide instruction, __KERNEL__ for Linux kernel builds
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Pure arithmetic (add/sub/mul/div/sqrt) is reentrant; with the default caches, fix16_exp, fix16_sin (and so fix16_cos) and fix16_atan2 read and write global cache index and value arrays without synchronisation, so concurrent or interrupt-time calls can race. Define FIXMATH_NO_CACHE for threads or ISRs.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: replacing float needs explicit conversions (fix16_from_float, fix16_to_float) and function calls in C; the C++ Fix16 class gives operators, but its default operators do raw int32 adds without overflow detection unless FIXMATH_SATURATING_ARITHMETIC is defined

gotchas: Correctness bug in the default build (found by reading libfixmath/fix16_exp.c at HEAD, unreported upstream): for a negative input fix16_exp negates inValue before storing it as the cache key, but stores it at the slot hashed from the original negative value. The hash (x ^ (x >> 4)) & 0xFFF is identical for x and -x exactly when x is a multiple of 0.5, so after fix16_exp(-2.0) a later fix16_exp(2.0) returns the cached exp(-2.0) = 0.135 instead of 7.389. This affects 19 inputs (0.5, 1.5, 2.0, ... 10.0; 1.0 is handled by an early return); negative inputs also never get a cache hit. FIXMATH_NO_CACHE avoids it, and fix16_exp has no unit tests (issue #43, open since 2023).

The overflow sentinel fix16_overflow is 0x80000000, the same bit pattern as fix16_minimum, so a legitimate result of -32768.0 is indistinguishable from an overflow; fix16_sadd(0, fix16_minimum) returns fix16_maximum (issue #53, open, May 2026).

fix16.h declares every function with __attribute__((leaf, nothrow, const)) on GCC newer than 4.6, including the cache-writing exp, sin and atan2, so the compiler may merge or move calls; the benchmark's MEASURE macro has no compiler barrier, which is how the float sqrtf and expf rows ended up at 8 cycles, and nothing guarantees the other rows' calls stayed inside the timer window.

fix16_sqrt of a negative input returns -sqrt(-x) instead of signalling an error; FIXMATH_NO_OVERFLOW turns fix16_add/sub into plain signed int32 adds (undefined behaviour on overflow in C); the CMake test matrix passes FIXMATH_NO_HARD_DIV while the library checks FIXMATH_NO_HARD_DIVISION, so its 12 '*div' variants do not exercise the software-division path except where FIXMATH_OPTIMIZE_8BIT forces it.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The other catalogued math entries (SLEEF, fmath, VDT, fast_math_cpp, xsimd) speed up float or double math on CPUs that have an FPU and SIMD; pick libfixmath only when there is no FPU or floating point is off-limits (AVR, Cortex-M0, kernel code), and keep float plus one of those libraries anywhere a hardware FPU exists.
verified_claims_summary: The only committed measurement is benchmarks/results-avr.ods (contributed in 2021): average cycles on a simulated ATmega128 (simulavr, avr-gcc -O2 -DFIXMATH_OPTIMIZE_8BIT, versions unstated) were fix16_add 67 versus 135 for soft-float add and fix16_sub 75 versus 135 (about 2x faster), but fix16_mul 377 versus 140 and fix16_div 637 versus 450 (slower). The test inputs are 50 operand pairs and 10 single operands drawn at random by generate_testcases.py (testcases.c is not committed, so the draw cannot be reproduced), overflow cases take early exits in fix16_mul, the 32 KB exp cache was left enabled on a 4 KB-SRAM part, and the float sqrtf/expf rows (8 cycles) are timing artifacts, so only the add/sub/mul/div rows are usable.
status_note: README says 'Not actively maintained, pull requests welcome', yet small fixes still land (2026-02-04, 2026-07-13) and CI builds 24 option variants; MIT and only a few source files, so it is easy to vendor, but build with FIXMATH_NO_CACHE given the unreported fix16_exp cache bug and the thread-unsafe caches.
